title: SSE anchored-chunk catalog and resume negotiation for semantic-framed streams
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Background: Our current SSE resume/reconnect work focuses on resume tokens and idempotent chunk IDs, but customers continue to see partial reconstructions when clients rejoin after network interruptions and when function/tool call frames interleave with text frames. This ticket proposes an anchored-chunk catalog approach plus a small negotiation handshake to make resume behavior deterministic across client libraries and proxies, and to preserve structured outputs (function calls) when fragments arrive out of order.

Goals:
- Reduce user-visible corruption on reconnects and partial retransmits (especially for functioncall JSON objects and structured outputs).
- Make resume deterministic: clients should be able to re-request missing anchors rather than rely on time-based heuristics.
- Provide clear backpressure hints so proxies and browsers can avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Maintain backwards compatibility with current resume-token based clients for a graceful rollout.

Proposed design (high level):
1) Anchored Chunk Catalog: every SSE event that represents a logical output fragment includes an anchor header (anchor-id) plus chunk-range (start, end) and a short provenance hash. The server maintains a transient per-session catalog mapping anchor-id -> {sequence ranges, provenance-hash, earliest-offset}. Catalog entries have TTL tied to session lifetime.

2) Semantic framing rules: fragments carry a semantic-type field (e.g., text, json-object, funcall, kv-cache-hint). Clients and proxies treat funcall fragments as atomic groups; individual fragments inside a funcall group are annotated with group-id + index so reassembly is deterministic.

3) Resume negotiation handshake: on reconnect, client sends last-known-anchor plus optional requested-anchor-list (explicit anchors it observed missing). Server responds with: a) resume-ack (server anchor pointer), b) patch instructions (serve missing anchor ranges inline or send compressed catalog pointers), or c) fall back to full resend for incompatible clients. The handshake uses short numeric tokens to minimize header bloat and is safe to pass through proxies.

4) Dedup and gap-heal using catalog: when receiving fragments after reconnect, client uses anchor-id + provenance-hash to deduplicate fragments and requests only gaps. This avoids replaying already-applied fragments and ensures funcall atomicity.

5) Backpressure and pacing hints: embed pace_hint (ms) and window tokens in event metadata so intermediate layers (edge, CDN, browser) can adapt delivery rate without affecting server internal batching. pace_hint is advisory and not prescriptive.

Compatibility and rollout strategy:
- Phase 1 (server opt-in): Server emits anchored headers and maintains catalog; older clients ignore unknown headers and continue using resume-token semantics.
- Phase 2 (client opt-in): Updated SDKs implement anchored catalog reconstructor and handshake. SDKs record observed anchors and proactively request missing anchors on reconnect.
- Phase 3 (strict mode): When both sides advertise support in handshake, server may stop sending full resend windows and rely on granulated patching to lower bandwidth cost.

Trade-offs considered:
- Catalog memory: keeping per-session catalogs increases memory. Mitigation: TTL eviction, size caps, and turning on catalog only for sessions exceeding a frag-rate threshold.
- Protocol complexity vs benefit: added headers increase parsing work for proxies. We keep header set minimal (anchor-id, group-id, chunk-range, provenance-hash, pace_hint).
- Backwards-compatibility: ensure older proxies ignore unknown headers by keeping everything SSE event-level (not custom http headers) and documenting graceful fallbacks.

Acceptance criteria:
- SDKs (JS, Python, Go) reconnect and reassemble streams with interleaved funcall frames without producing duplicate or corrupted structured outputs in >95% of simulated flakiness tests.
- Bandwidth savings: when strict-mode enabled, avg resend bytes per reconnect drop by >60% on synthetic workloads.
- No regressing existing resume-token clients: regression test against legacy clients must pass.

Testing plan:
- Unit: chunk catalog serialization/parsing, anchoring dedupe logic, handshake path variations.
- Integration: harness with flaky network simulator (latency/jitter/drop patterns) and functioncall-heavy transcripts.
- Load test: cluster-level memory and catalog eviction under 100k concurrent sessions.
- E2E: staged rollout on canary region with metrics: reconnect-error-rate, structured-output-corruption, avg-resend-bytes.

Rollout plan:
- Merge server feature flag behind runtime-anchored-sse.
- Release opt-in SDKs with feature flag off by default.
- Enable for a small set of internal customers and benchmark.
- After 2 weeks of stable telemetry, open opt-in to 10% of traffic, then 50% then 100% with monitoring gates.

Docs & artifacts:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Anchored+Chunk+Catalog+Design
- Initial implementation PR (server): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4128
- JS SDK partial client: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/pull/879
- Test harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/stream-tests/tree/anchored-catalog

Open questions / discussion items:
- Should provenance-hash be SHA256 or a shorter blake2b-64? Shorter hashes reduce wire size but increase collision risk for long-lived sessions.
- What catalog size cap is acceptable before we revert to full resend? Recommendation: 2KB per active session by default, configurable.
- How to surface diagnostics for customer support when reassembly fails? Suggest adding a per-session reassembly trace blob accessible from Console for 7 days.
